evals.prompt: We have not implemented this delivery workflow yet. Model the proposal in delivery-design.md, compare it with the stable-ID alternative, and tell me which guarantees depend on unresolved assumptions. Leave a runnable model and explanation; do not implement the service.
evals.expected_output: A design model with explicit assumptions, checked safety and qualified progress claims, constructed scenarios, and design findings rather than invented implementation bugs or source traces.
expectations: The artifact contains a runnable formal model and executed checks for the proposed workflow and stable-ID alternative.
The report distinguishes a design counterexample from a confirmed implementation bug and does not fabricate implementation source locations or observed traces.
The original workflow has a demonstrated duplicate-notification behaviour, and the stable-ID result explicitly depends on remote deduplication semantics.
Progress claims state scheduling and recovery/delivery assumptions or explicitly remain unverified.
No service implementation is created, and a useful model plus explanation remains available.

evals.prompt: Model lifecycle.py so we can understand its behaviour and check the contract in lifecycle-contract.md. I have no suspected bug. Leave a runnable model that we can maintain alongside the code; do not change the implementation.
evals.expected_output: A faithful model of all transitions including no-ops, reachability and implementation correspondence evidence, checked at-most-once and absorbing terminal properties, no fabricated defect, and no unpromised completion guarantee.
expectations: A runnable formal model covers start, finish, cancel and ignored/duplicate events, with executed checks.
The at-most-one-start and absorbing-terminal properties are supported by actual model checks or completed proofs, with their limits stated.
The model demonstrates a reachable running or terminal outcome and compares at least one observed implementation trace or shared-input result.
No defect or unconditional eventual-completion guarantee is invented.
The input lifecycle.py remains byte-for-byte unchanged and rerun instructions are supplied.

evals.prompt: Use a formal model to check worker.py against worker-contract.md, and fix any implementation defect you can reproduce. Leave the model and a deterministic regression test. Keep the scope to this in-memory workflow.
evals.expected_output: A model that retains the suspension gap, a concrete interleaving, a failing real-code reproducer, a scoped fix, passing regression and before/after model evidence with explicit bounds.
expectations: The model preserves the before_claim suspension gap and produces a concrete duplicate-send counterexample.
A deterministic real-code test or reproducer fails on the original for the modelled reason.
A scoped fix passes the same regression test without timing sleeps.
Before/after formal results and relevant source mappings support the reported fix.
The final report respects the one-event-loop contract and distinguishes model bounds from implementation evidence.

evals.prompt: TLC passes on our spec in claim.tla with claim.cfg. Tell me whether that result means claim.py is safe against claim-contract.md, and leave the model in a state we can rerun. Do not change claim.py.
evals.expected_output: Recognition that the passing run is vacuous (Claim never fires), a corrected model that reaches the duplicate send, a named reachability check that would have caught the vacuity, and no safety or defect claim about claim.py from the model alone.
expectations: Detects that the Claim action never fires or the send state is unreachable (via a reachability check or coverage), and does not report the passing run as evidence of safety.
Corrects the model and shows the duplicate send is then reachable.
Leaves an expected-failure check that would have caught the vacuity, naming the violation it expects.
Treats the implementation race as a candidate unless reproduced against claim.py, and does not claim claim.py is safe or unsafe on the strength of the model alone.
claim.py remains byte-for-byte unchanged and rerun instructions are supplied.

evals.prompt: Prove the claim in retry-claim.md about retry.py in Lean. If it is false, show me why.
evals.expected_output: A concrete sequence of send outcomes that makes deliver call send more than max_retries + 1 times, stated and proved as a Lean theorem, with any corrected claim labelled as a different statement.
expectations: Produces a concrete sequence of send outcomes (involving throttled errors) that violates the claim.
A Lean theorem stating that violation builds, with no sorry and no native_decide.
Does not present an unfinished or failed proof attempt as the answer.
Any corrected or weakened claim that is proved is labelled as a different statement from the one asked.
The report distinguishes the model's result from behaviour of retry.py itself, and states how the model corresponds to the code.

evals.prompt: Use a formal model to check worker.py against worker-contract.md, and fix any implementation defect you can reproduce. Leave the model and a deterministic regression test. Keep the scope to this in-memory workflow. Installing or downloading tools is not authorized.
evals.expected_output: The same outcome as case 3 where the tools are installed, found without being told where they are; otherwise an exact account of where it looked and a model labelled unexecuted.
expectations: Locates an installed Java and TLC jar (or Lean toolchain) without being given their paths, or states exactly where it looked before concluding one is missing.
Does not claim a model check ran unless one did, and installs nothing.
If the tools are present, the model check and the regression test run as in case 3.
